name: Bird's Opening
summary: White controls the key central square from the side with a pawn, a knight and a long-range bishop, then castles into a safe, flexible setup.

goal.title: Take control of the key central square
goal.text: White's side pawn and a knight both watch the square in front of Black's central pawns, and the bishop soon joins them from the long diagonal. Meanwhile White tucks the king away early and keeps a solid, compact setup. From that safe base White decides when to break open the center.
plans: Use the side pawn and a knight to control the key central square (marked on the board).
Put the bishop on the long diagonal so it also eyes that square and the far corner.
Castle early and keep the pawns in front of the king solid.
Once the pieces are out, break open the center with a central pawn push, or plant a knight on the key square.

variations.name: Main line: 1...d5 (Black builds a classical center)
variations.strategy: The middlegame is a fight over the key central square. Your side pawn, knight and long-diagonal bishop all watch it, so aim to trade off the Black piece that guards it and then take the square with a knight or a pawn. Black's fianchettoed bishop sits on the same long diagonal as yours, so a trade of those bishops is a natural moment to ease the pressure. Once the center is settled, swing the queen toward the king side and lift a rook along the third rank to attack the Black king. Black's counterplay comes from the center pawn push, which blunts your bishop, and from the e-pawn break, so keep the pawns in front of your king solid.

variations.name: From's Gambit: 1...e5 (Black offers a pawn)
variations.strategy: You are a pawn up but Black has open lines, so the middlegame is about safety first and the extra pawn second. Black's rook looks down the open file at your king-side pawns and a bishop eyes your king, so finish development, get the king-side bishop out and only castle when the attack has been blunted (castling on the other side is a real option). Trade the most dangerous Black pieces, then use the open file for your own rook against Black's weak pawn, and let the extra pawn decide the endgame.

variations.name: Vs 1...Nf6: a flexible kingside setup
variations.strategy: The pawns on the f, e and d files form a compact wedge that takes space from Black's knights. Black's d-pawn covers the key central square, so a knight cannot settle there yet; use the wedge for space and prepare the e-pawn advance instead. Bring the other knight to the third rank and develop the dark-squared bishop on the queen side or to the second rank to support the center, since your d-pawn closes the long diagonal. Black's usual plan is a side-pawn push against your center, so keep your pieces placed to answer it, and consider a king-side attack with the queen and a rook lift.

variations.name: Main line with ...c5: Black hits the center from the side
variations.strategy: Black has grabbed space in the center with three pawns, so the middlegame is about showing that this space is a target, not a strength. Your knight and long-diagonal bishop already watch the key central square: jump a knight there to force trades and make Black's pieces defend. If Black pushes the center pawn to cramp you, answer with a pawn lever on the side or the e-file break rather than waiting. Keep the king safe behind its pawns and aim for a king-side attack once Black's key defenders, the king-side knight and the dark-squared bishop, have been traded or driven away. The line vs the side-pawn first move ends in this same position.

variations.name: Vs 1...c5: the Sicilian-style reply
variations.strategy: This reaches exactly the same position as the line where Black plays the center pawn first, so play it the same way. Black's realistic way to cramp your long-diagonal bishop is the center pawn push; meet it by trading on that square with the e-pawn or striking with the c-pawn. If Black instead pushes the side pawn forward, simply win it. Keep the knight ready to jump to the key central square and start the king-side attack with the queen swing, because Black's king is where your pieces point.

variations.name: Vs 1...g6: Black copies the fianchetto
variations.strategy: Black has fianchettoed a bishop and has just hit your central pawn from the side. Decide whether to support the pawn or to trade and open the position for your pieces. Black's pawn on the sixth rank covers the key central square, so a knight cannot sit there for now; control it with pawns and pieces and prepare the e-pawn advance. Watch Black's bishop pointing at your queen side, and start play on the king side with the queen and a pawn advance once the center is settled.

variations.name: Vs 1...e6: Black builds a solid, closed structure
variations.strategy: Both of your bishops point at Black's king: one on the long diagonal and one aimed at the king side. Plant a knight on the key central square, swing the queen over, and look for a king-side attack; if Black's defenders get overloaded, a bishop sacrifice on the king-side pawn can crack open the king. Black's counterplay comes from a central pawn break and a knight jump to the center, so answer with the other knight and keep a pawn in front of your king.

variations.name: 1...d5 2.Nf3 Nc6: Black develops fast and pins the knight
variations.strategy: Black's pieces came out fast, so the middlegame is about not letting that early activity turn into an attack on your f-pawn. Count the attackers and defenders on it, and keep a pawn and a piece defending it. If Black trades the bishop for your knight, you get the bishop pair whichever way you recapture, so open the position later to use it. Then control the key central square, develop the long-diagonal bishop, and look for a break in the center once Black's pieces have run out of useful squares.

variations.name: Vs 1...f5: the Dutch-style reply
variations.strategy: Both sides have the f-pawn forward, but the setups differ: you hold the center with the d- and e-pawns, while Black has fianchettoed and keeps the d-pawn back. You are a move ahead, so use it: expand with a central or side pawn before Black does, develop the knights to the third rank, and prepare to swing the queen to the king side. Black's fianchettoed bishop looks along the long diagonal toward your queen side, so do not weaken that side carelessly.

variations.name: Vs 1...d6: a modest reply
variations.strategy: This reaches exactly the same position as the line where Black fianchettoes first, so play it the same way. Black's setup is flexible and there is nothing to punish, so the middlegame is about slow, safe improvement. When Black hits your central pawn, either support it with a pawn or trade and use the open file. Control the key central square with pawns and pieces, bring the knights to good squares, and expand on the queen side or push on the king side with the queen. Do not rush an attack before your pieces are placed.

variations.name: Vs 1...Nc6: develop first
variations.strategy: Black's knight and center pawn make a classical setup, so the middlegame depends on who controls the center. You have the extra tempo, so challenge Black's central pawn with a pawn lever or a knight jump to the key central square. Keep the long-diagonal bishop pointing at the center, swing the queen to the king side, and be ready to answer Black's pawn break with a trade rather than letting the center pawn become a hook for Black's pieces.

variations.name: Vs 1...d5 2.Nf3 Bf5: stay calm
variations.strategy: Black's light-squared bishop sits outside the pawn chain and eyes your queen side and the central light squares, so the middlegame is about challenging or trading it. Aim a knight at it, control the central squares so it has little to bite on, and prepare a pawn push to gain space. Once the bishop is dealt with, use the long-diagonal bishop and the key central square to build pressure on the center.

variations.name: Vs 1...d5 2.Nf3 e6: the solid setup
variations.strategy: Black's pawn on the side hits the center, but Black's light-squared bishop is stuck behind its own pawns. Your bishop aims at the king-side and the long-diagonal bishop supports a knight jump to the key central square, so combine them with a queen swing for an attack. Do not place your center pawn too early where Black can attack it: keep the structure flexible and break only when your pieces are ready.
